facts.text: The RAND argument is the finding from a 2016 RAND Corporation report that proving a self-driving car is as safe as a human driver through driving alone would require hundreds of millions to billions of miles, far more than any fleet can drive.
facts.quote: proving a self-driving car is as safe as a human driver by simply driving it would take hundreds of millions to billions of miles, far more than any fleet can drive.

facts.text: At the time of RAND's 2016 report, the human-driver fatal crash rate in the United States was about 1.09 per 100 million miles.
facts.quote: Fatal crashes are rare: about 1.09 per 100 million miles for human drivers in the United States at the time of the report.

facts.text: Showing with 95 percent confidence that a self-driving car's fatality rate is no worse than the human-driver benchmark of about 1.09 per 100 million miles would require about 275 million miles without a fatality.
facts.quote: To show, with 95 percent confidence, that a self-driving car's fatality rate is no worse than that, the car would have to drive about 275 million miles without a fatality.

facts.text: Showing that a self-driving car's fatality rate is 20 percent better than the human-driver benchmark, with 95 percent confidence and 80 percent power, would require about 11 billion miles.
facts.quote: To show that it is 20 percent better, with 95 percent confidence and 80 percent power, would take about 11 billion miles.

facts.text: Driving to Safety by Kalra and Paddock, published in April 2016, concluded that existing fleets would need tens and sometimes hundreds of years to drive the distances needed for the self-driving safety comparisons.
facts.quote: The report, Driving to Safety by Kalra and Paddock (April 2016), concluded that existing fleets would need "tens and sometimes hundreds of years" to drive such distances

facts.text: For heavy machines, real operating hours alone cannot demonstrate rare-event performance; claims about rare misses must rely on stratified testing, simulation volume and a credibility argument.
facts.quote: The logic transfers to heavy machines: real operating hours alone cannot demonstrate rare-event performance, so a claim about rare misses must come from stratified testing, simulation volume and a credibility argument

facts.text: The RAND mileage numbers do not transfer to off-road validation: the on-road claim concerns a fatality rate per mile that can only be observed by driving, whereas the off-road claim concerns detection and intervention per encounter.
facts.quote: The numbers do not transfer. The on-road claim is a fatality rate per mile, which can only be observed by driving. The off-road claim is about detection and intervention per encounter

facts.text: Off-road detection and intervention encounters can be staged on a test pad and run in simulation many thousands of times; this difference from on-road fatality-rate validation makes the four-month plan conceivable.
facts.quote: encounters can be staged on a test pad and run in simulation many thousands of times. That difference is what makes the four-month plan conceivable

facts.text: The booklet treats the inability of field exposure alone to demonstrate rare-event performance as a well-established finding, with RAND as its clearest statement; the program therefore cannot establish performance simply by running machines on customer sites and counting events.
facts.quote: The booklet lists "field exposure alone cannot demonstrate rare-event performance" among its well-established findings and uses RAND as the clearest statement of it. It is the reason the program cannot simply run machines on customer sites and count
